transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-07-22
Start time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~72 mins
Attendees: Amelia Chen (Redwood AE), Rafael Ortiz (Redwood SE), Priya N. (Redwood), Jordan Miles (Ceres IT Ops), Dr. Sana Kapoor (Ceres ML Ops), Liam O'Rourke (Ceres Sec), Maya Chen (Platform)

Summary: quick run-through of air-gapped artifact transport, driver validation, offline license activation, and a proposed perf checklist. Focus on checksums, signed packages, and KV cache warmup strategies.

[00:00] Amelia: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros, then we'll dive into the offline artifact flow. Rafael's going to walk through the driver/packaging bits.
[00:34] Jordan: Hi, uh, Jordan here — we run a mostly air-gapped cluster, couple of racks, DGX-ish boxes, a mix of A100 40GB and some older A6000s. we want to ensure we get the exact driver stack that you certify.
[00:50] Rafael: great, thanks. quick note — our private agent package is a signed tarball, we publish sha256 sums and a gpg signature. in an air-gap, we provide an offline bundle that contains: the runtime binaries, docker images as oci tarballs, kernel modules if needed, and the offline license file.
[01:18] Liam: when you say signed, is that with your company gpg key? we need to escalate to our key mgmt for verification and possibly re-signing.
[01:28] Priya: yes, we sign with Redwood's package key and provide the public key fingerprint so you can verify. For regulated setups you can import and verify against your HSM. we also support a workflow where you re-sign with your internal key after verification.
[01:45] Dr. Sana: is there a way to prove integrity on the host without internet? checksums ok but we want a chain-of-trust.
[01:55] Rafael: absolutely, we provide the tar.gz, a .sha256 file and a .sig (gpg). you can import our public key and verify locally: gpg --verify. we include a note in the runbook about key fingerprints and recommend using an offline hardware token if you want to store the signing key, or use your HSM to re-sign like Priya mentioned.
[02:20] Amelia: also we'll provide the license activation mechanics — offline activation is a two-step exchange: you place the license request file on a transfer medium, we return an activation blob that you apply locally. no outbound calls needed.
[02:38] Jordan: transfer mediums... are we talking secure usb drives? we have policy for removable media — file scanning
[02:44] Maya: yes we prefer locked transport, md5/sha256 checksums, and chain of custody forms.
[02:52] Rafael: recommended: use an encrypted external drive, transfer via an intermediate verified host (a jumpbox), checksum after copy, then gpg verify. we'll supply an example chain-of-custody PDF with signatures.
[03:05] [small crosstalk] Speaker 1: (inaudible)
[03:20] Amelia: ok onto drivers — what we've tested: driver combos for CUDA 12.1 + cuDNN 9.x on A100. we also have validated a fallback on 11.8 for older nodes. important to match kernel versions.
[03:40] Jordan: our rhel kernels vary — some nodes are 4.18, a couple are custom-compiled 5.14. driver kernel module rebuilds are fine but we need instructions.
[03:53] Rafael: we'll include dkms scripts in the bundle and a step-by-step for rebuilding. note: if your kernel has a custom config we recommend a preflight check script we provide. it will check for gcc version mismatch, kernel-headers, and existing nvidia module conflicts.
[04:18] Liam: are there signed kernel module concerns for rhel? we enforce module signing policy.
[04:25] Priya: we can provide our kernel module with a signing key or provide instructions to sign it with your internal key; both supported. we'll call out the kmod signing steps in the runbook.
[04:40] [05:01] Rafael: on the runtime side — the Redwood Private runtime has a KV cache for attention key/value states. for long-response workloads you should pre-warm the KV cache to avoid cold-start latencies. that means replaying common prefixes or using our warmup tool included in the bundle.
[05:20] Jordan: what's the typical warmup volume to see <10ms incremental token latency?
[05:28] Rafael: depends on model and kv size — generally a few hundred to a few thousand tokens per model shard per GPU. we'll share a small harness to drive the warmup; for perf runs we recommend parallel warmup across GPUs to populate local KV.
[05:47] Dr. Sana: can KV be persisted across process restarts? our maintenance windows kill daemons often.
[05:55] Rafael: persistence is supported if you enable the local snapshotting feature — the runtime writes kv snapshots to a configured path and reloads on startup. space on disk is needed — we document the estimated size per model and sequence length.
[06:12] Amelia: note: snapshotting is on by opt-in in air-gapped installs due to disk usage and we can provide tuning knobs — eviction policy, snapshot frequency.
[06:29] [06:45] Jordan: batching and latency — we need to support 150 RPS with 50 token average responses, 95th latency <200ms. is that realistic on our hardware?
[06:54] Rafael: with dedicated pools and optimized kernels yes. three levers: batching window, max-batch-size, and kv locality. For low-p99 latency, reduce batching window and keep batch sizes smaller, but throughput suffers. We'll provide a recommended config for your QPS/latency targets.
[07:16] Maya: quantization — we want to push cost down. do you support int8 or 4-bit? what's the tradeoff?
[07:23] Priya: we support several quant profiles. 8-bit quant (int8) gives good perf wins with minimal quality loss for many models. 4-bit/QLoRA style quantization provides more savings but you may see occasional degradations. we include eval scripts so you can run your prompt set after quantizing to check regressions.
[07:47] Dr. Sana: we absolutely need integration with our eval suite — can you provide a sample evaluation pipeline in the bundle?
[07:53] Rafael: yes, there's a small python harness that runs your prompts, computes rouge/bleu/embedding-sim/semantic-sim and highlights regressions. it'll run locally without external calls.
[08:11] [08:30] Liam: security review — logging and audit. how are audit logs exported from a private deployment in an air-gapped environment?
[08:37] Priya: logs are written to local disk and we provide a log-shipper binary that can push to your internal SIEM over your private network. for air-gapped you can schedule periodic pull jobs or transfer compressed logs out via secure media. all log entries are signed with per-instance keys if you enable that.
[08:58] Jordan: retention policies? we need 7 years for some telemetry fields.
[09:04] Amelia: we document retention knobs and recommend sending token-level traces only when necessary; cost and storage are large. by default we keep operational traces shorter and have a separate archival tool to offload to your tape or object store.
[09:27] [09:45] Rafael: performance tuning notes: for throughput we prefer using continuous batching + dynamic kernel selection. the runtime will choose kernels based on sequence length distribution. for very short context (<=64) different kernels win than long-context (>=1024). we include benchmarks we ran to show which kernel to pin for your expected distribution.
[10:12] Dr. Sana: about model rollouts — do we lose the ability to do canary if we're fully air-gapped?
[10:20] Priya: you can still do canaries internally by running two runtime instances with different model versions and routing traffic via your internal load balancer. Redwood's rollout tooling can generate the config artifacts that you apply locally; the control plane operations (if you choose not to run the control plane locally) are just files and scripts.
[10:42] Jordan: what about fallback to hosted if we lose capacity? not possible in a strict air-gap.
[10:48] Amelia: correct, fallback requires outbound connectivity. for strict air-gapped customers we offer a high-availability configuration with reserved capacity across racks, and suggested on-prem scaling patterns to avoid needing hosted fallback.
[11:00] [11:20] Maya: driver versions again — do you pin drivers at install time? or can we upgrade in place?
[11:26] Rafael: we ship the validated driver version and recommend pinning initially; upgrades are supported via the same offline bundle process. we include a compatibility matrix per model.
[11:40] [12:02] Dr. Sana: about license activation - how granular is licensing? per-node, per-GPU, or per-cluster?
[12:09] Priya: license SKUs are flexible — per-cluster baseline plus per-GPU entitlements for peak capacity. offline license file expresses the node identifiers and GPU serials; the activation blob is tied to that fingerprint. we also support time-limited trial activations.
[12:33] Liam: can we run license verification against our local KMS?
[12:38] Rafael: yes — license verification can be integrated with your local KMS for key storage. the activation uses asymmetric crypto so the private key never leaves your HSM.
[12:55] [13:20] Jordan: onboarding window — what do you need from us to prep?
[13:28] Amelia: the checklist: exact node counts and GPU SKUs, kernel versions, offline transfer mechanism approvals, and a security contact. Rafael will need access to a staging node (we'll coordinate via jumpbox during the install window).
[13:46] Maya: our compliance team needs the shipper of the media to sign chain forms. can you provide templated docs?
[13:53] Priya: yes - chain-of-custody and transfer templates included.
[14:05] [14:35] Rafael: perf run details — we'll run three phases: 1) driver/module validation, 2) KV warmup and sustained throughput ramp, 3) latency p99 sweeps under load. we'll bring a small benchmark harness that runs in local mode and outputs token-per-second, memory, and kv hit ratio.
[14:58] Dr. Sana: what about measuring the impact of quantization on latency?
[15:05] Rafael: quantization generally reduces memory bandwidth and improves throughput; our harness will run both quantized and fp16 variants back-to-back so you can see deltas. we log quality deltas too.
[15:25] [15:50] Jordan: any special NIC or rdma requirement? we do have mellanox cards.
[15:58] Rafael: RDMA helps for multi-node KV sharing patterns. if you plan to do model sharding across nodes with KV fetch across network, RDMA + GPUDirect is recommended. we'll include recommended MTU and resource limits.
[16:20] Maya: storage requirements for snapshotting? ballpark numbers?
[16:26] Rafael: depends on model and sequence length. e.g., for the 30B model at 1024 seq, expect ~6-8GB per GPU for KV snapshot; we'll provide exact numbers per model variant in the bundle.
[16:45] [17:10] Amelia: ok let's talk about artifact naming conventions so it's easy to verify on your side. we use: redwood-private-v{version}-{model}-{platform}-{sha256:.8}.tar.gz and accompanying .sha256 and .sig files.
[17:32] Jordan: please include human-readable manifest with file sizes.
[17:37] Rafael: will do. also, we can provide a quick python script that verifies all checksums and signatures in one go.
[17:50] [18:20] Dr. Sana: downtime for installing drivers — what's realistic?
[18:26] Rafael: for replacing kernel modules you may need host reboots per node; with rolling installs and live-migration you'll aim for minimal disruption. we provide recommended maintenance-window commands.
[18:45] Liam: policy question — do you collect any telemetry by default from Private?
[18:51] Priya: no telemetry leaves your network by default; optional reporting features are explicitly off in air-gapped installs. we document what ops logs look like and how to enable them if you choose.
[19:10] [19:40] Amelia: quick note — because this is an air-gapped customer we'll create a bespoke bundle and sign it with an ephemeral key; we will also provide instructions for you to re-sign.
[19:55] Jordan: we need the driver validation checklist earlier so our infra team can pre-approve.
[20:02] Rafael: I'll send that today. it includes kernel header versions, gcc, dkms steps, and a known-issues section.
[20:18] [20:45] Maya: about the license blob size — is it privacy sensitive? we want to review the payload.
[20:51] Priya: the license blob contains encrypted metadata (node ids, gpu serials) and a signature; we can provide a redacted sample for legal review. no customer data is included.
[21:10] Dr. Sana: for benchmarking, would you run with 1 or multiple model replicas per GPU?
[21:18] Rafael: typically we recommend one replica per GPU for large models; for smaller models you can pack multiple. packing affects KV locality and batching behavior. we'll recommend an optimal mapping for your mix of A100/A6000.
[21:40] [22:05] Jordan: any special system settings? hugepages? swappiness?
[22:12] Rafael: yes — we recommend setting swappiness to 1, configure hugepages for the runtime if you expect large tokenizer memory, and adjust file descriptor limits. details are in the sysctl section.
[22:36] Maya: time sync—our policy is strict NTP sources blocked, we use internal time servers. licence activation timestamp skew concerns?
[22:45] Amelia: the license activation window tolerates a few minutes skew; we do include unix timestamp and allow configurable skew on the server side. we'll document the exact tolerance.
[23:05] [23:30] Dr. Sana: troubleshooting checklist for perf regressions?
[23:36] Rafael: 1) confirm correct driver/cuda/cuDNN; 2) verify kernel modules; 3) check KV hit ratio; 4) analyze batching distribution (are you seeing giant batches causing latency spikes); 5) check for noisy neighbors on host. we'll include a script that dumps these metrics.
[23:58] Jordan: could you share a minimal set of metrics we should store long-term?
[24:04] Priya: token-per-second, kv-hit-rate, avg-latency, p95/p99, memory-alloc per GPU, and oom events.
[24:24] [24:50] Amelia: ok, recap and next steps. We'll: 1) prepare and send the offline bundle and signed checksums, 2) send driver validation checklist, 3) propose install window Aug 4-8, 4) provide perf harness and warmup scripts.
[25:10] Jordan: confirmed, we'll reply with node inventory and security contacts by Friday.
[25:22] Dr. Sana: we'll also provide the prompt set for evals and perf goals.
[25:30] Liam: security will review the sample license payload before activation.
[25:36] Amelia: perfect. last question — any show-stoppers?
[25:41] Jordan: nothing immediate. the only sticky part will be chain-of-custody approval for removable media.
[25:48] Priya: we'll add the exact paperwork templates and the shipping checklist.
[26:00] [26:30] Speaker 2: (inaudible)
[26:48] Amelia: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the bundle and meeting notes.

-- End meeting --

Notes on transcript quality: medium. occasional inaudible segments and speaker mislabels.

Attachments referenced: redwood-offline-bundle-v1.2.tar.gz (will be delivered via secure SFTP), driver-validation-checklist.pdf, chain-of-custody-template.pdf, perf-harness.zip, example-license-request.txt
